Features

the meaning behind the names — every section of Canopus is drawn from Hindu tradition, Vedic astronomy, and mythology
Focus
Alcyone (Main Focus)
Hindu association: Krittika Nakshatra
Krittika is associated with courage, discipline, and unwavering resolve — a reminder that achievement is never the result of talent alone, but of the willingness to confront discomfort, remain committed, and continue despite distractions. Focus is named Alcyone because every meaningful pursuit begins with a choice: to set aside excuses, embrace responsibility, and dedicate oneself completely to the task at hand.
Courage · Discipline · Determination · Resilience
Sky
Polaris (Sky)
Hindu association: Dhruva
Known in Hindu tradition as Dhruva, Polaris has long been a symbol of constancy and purpose — remaining steadfast while countless stars appear to move across the night sky, guiding generations of travelers. Sky is named Polaris because the heavens have always inspired humanity to explore beyond the familiar; every discovery begins by looking upward and asking questions.
Guidance · Purpose · Exploration · Constancy
Capsule
Pushya (Capsule)
Hindu association: Pushya Nakshatra
Pushya, governed by Brihaspati — the guru of the gods — is one of the most revered nakshatras in Vedic tradition, symbolizing learning, wisdom, growth, and blessings; its very name means "to nourish." Capsule is built on a simple belief: great knowledge is not acquired all at once but through countless small lessons accumulated over time, each one a seed of understanding.
Learning · Wisdom · Growth · Nourishment · Blessings
Vault
Canopus (Knowledge Vault)
Hindu association: Agastya
In Hindu tradition, the brilliant star Canopus is identified with the great sage Agastya, whose wisdom, scholarship, and contributions to civilization have been revered for millennia — remembered not for conquest, but for expanding the frontiers of human understanding. The Vault carries this name because knowledge is humanity's greatest inheritance, preserved here not simply as information to be stored, but as wisdom to be explored, understood, and passed forward.
Wisdom · Scholarship · Discovery · Preservation · Enlightenment
Open Vault
Empires
Regulus (Empires)
Hindu association: Magha Nakshatra
Regulus, "the little king," has been read as a royal star across nearly every ancient sky-watching tradition. In Hindu astronomy it anchors Magha — "the mighty one" — the nakshatra of thrones, ancestry, and inherited authority, ruled by the Pitrs, the spirits of one's forebears. Empires is named Regulus because every empire mapped here is exactly that — authority built on what preceded it, extending outward until it reshaped the map, and eventually passing, as all thrones do, to something else. Explore the peak territory, GDP, and history of history's greatest empires — from Maurya and Mughal India to Rome, the Mongols, and beyond — on a rotating globe.
Power · Legacy · Ambition · Ancestry · Rise & Fall
Open Empires
Conflicts
Antares (Conflicts)
Hindu association: Jyeshtha Nakshatra
Antares is Scorpius's fiery red heart, and in Hindu astronomy it anchors Jyeshtha — "the eldest" — the nakshatra of seniority, protection, and hard-won authority, ruled by Indra, king of the gods and wielder of the thunderbolt against chaos. Conflicts is named Antares because every war mapped here is guarded ground fought over by rival claims to seniority and protection — each one, in some real sense, the unfinished business of the one before it. Trace fifteen major world conflicts on a rotating globe, then follow the branching flowchart of how each one caused the next.
History · Causality · Power · Seniority · Consequence
Open Conflicts
Literature
Venus (Literature)
Hindu association: Shukra
In Hindu tradition, Shukra (Venus) is celebrated as one of the greatest masters of knowledge, renowned for command of literature, poetry, philosophy, aesthetics, diplomacy, and the Shastras — representing the understanding that knowledge is not confined to facts alone, but also lives in beauty, language, and imagination. Literature is named Venus because stories are among humanity's greatest achievements: they preserve civilizations, challenge beliefs, inspire revolutions, and let one generation speak to the next across centuries.
Literature · Poetry · Philosophy · Culture · Aesthetics
LOQ
Sirius (Library of Quotation)
Hindu association: Mrigavyadha
Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is known in Hindu tradition as Mrigavyadha — "the deer hunter" — prized for its unmistakable brilliance and precision, cutting through the dark with a clarity no other star can match. LOQ is named Sirius because a single well-aimed sentence can do the same: a great quotation is thought distilled to its brightest, sharpest point. This library gathers those points of light from history's sharpest minds, organised into subsections so the right words are always easy to find.
Wisdom · Brevity · Insight · Memory · Clarity
Open LOQ
Library
Mercury (Library of Philosophy & Speeches)
Hindu association: Budha
In Hindu astrology, Budha (Mercury) is the swift, articulate prince of the gods — ruler of intellect, discernment, and the spoken word. Where Venus gives knowledge its beauty, Mercury gives it its edge: the reasoned argument, the closely built system of thought, the speech that moves a crowd or bends the course of history. The Library is named Mercury because clear thinking and clear speech have always been how humanity argues its way toward truth — gathering the world's great schools of philosophy and its most consequential speeches under one roof.
Reason · Rhetoric · Discernment · Argument · Eloquence
Open Library
A journey through knowledge

Together, these names tell the story of learning itself. It begins with Alcyone, where courage and discipline turn intention into action. It looks to Polaris, the constant guide that reminds us every explorer needs a direction. It grows through Pushya, where every small lesson becomes another step toward wisdom. It culminates in Canopus, the great repository of human understanding, preserving the knowledge that defines civilization. It finds its soul in Venus, where literature, philosophy, and art remind us that knowledge is meant not only to inform the mind, but also to move the heart. It sharpens to a point in Sirius, where the wisdom of history's greatest voices is distilled into single, unforgettable lines. And it learns to argue and articulate in Mercury, where the great schools of philosophy and the speeches that changed history show reasoning and rhetoric at their sharpest.

Welcome to Canopus
Your focused day, beautifully structured

Canopus is a minimal day-planning tool with three core experiences — a distraction-free clock, a session scheduler, and a focus timer. Here's a quick look at what you can do.

Focus Mode
A clean full-screen clock. Click the time to track elapsed time from a reference point. Switch between Clock and Elapsed views.
Schedule
Build a day of named sessions with start/end times. Watch your timeline fill in as the day progresses. Sessions auto-highlight when they're live.
Focus Timer
Set countdown timers, save presets, and launch a fullscreen timer overlay. Supports Pomodoro-style work and break cycles.
Flight Mode
Track a live flight on an animated globe. Enter departure and arrival airport codes, set flight duration, and watch your progress in real time.

Focus mode keeps your attention on the present moment — nothing but the time and optionally, how long you've been at it.

1
Navigate to Focus using the top nav bar.
2
Click the large clock to start tracking elapsed time from that moment. Click again to reset.
3
Hover over the small bar below the clock to switch between Clock mode and Elapsed mode.
4
If you have sessions in Schedule, a progress bar at the bottom shows the current active session.
5
Use the expand icon (bottom-right) to jump directly into the fullscreen timer from Focus view.

Build your day by adding named sessions. Canopus tracks them on a live timeline and highlights what's active right now.

1
Go to Schedule and click + Add session in the left panel.
2
Enter a name, pick a category (Study, Work, Break, Exercise), and set start & end times using the clock picker.
3
Sessions appear in the left list and as coloured segments on the day timeline on the right.
4
The currently active session glows with a white left-border and its progress bar fills live.
5
Click the × on any session card to delete it. Stats (total sessions, hours planned) update automatically.

The timer panel in Schedule lets you run focused work blocks with presets, quick durations, and a fullscreen countdown mode.

1
On the Schedule page, find the Timer panel on the right side. Switch between Presets and Active tabs.
2
Click + Add preset to save a named timer (e.g. "Deep Work — 45 min"). Hit the play icon to start any preset instantly.
3
Use the quick duration chips (5, 10, 25 min…) to start a timer without saving a preset.
4
Press T or the expand icon to open the fullscreen timer overlay — great for display on a second monitor.
5
In fullscreen mode, choose a Schedule session to link the timer directly to a block from your day plan.

Flight mode turns Canopus into a personal flight tracker — handy when you're on a long-haul flight and want to watch your progress on a spinning globe.

1
In fullscreen timer mode, select the Flight tab (look for the plane icon chip).
2
Enter your departure and arrival airport codes (e.g. DEL → LHR). The app searches a built-in airport database.
3
Select your flight duration using the duration chips or manual input, then hit Start.
4
A 3D globe animates your plane's position in real time. The HUD shows elapsed time, ETA, and destination local time.
5
Move your cursor to reveal the HUD customiser — adjust position, scale, and which info fields to show.

A few shortcuts and hidden touches to help you get the most from Canopus.

Keyboard Shortcuts
Press Esc to close overlays, modals, and panels.
Light / Dark Theme
Click the sun/moon icon in the top-right nav to switch between dark and light themes. Your preference is remembered across sessions.
True Fullscreen
The maximize icon in the nav puts your browser into true fullscreen — perfect for using Canopus as a dedicated display on a second screen or desk monitor.
Auto-hide Controls
In the fullscreen timer and flight overlay, controls fade out after a few seconds of inactivity. Move your mouse to bring them back — keeping the view clean by default.

Alfred is a local AI assistant built into the Terminal, powered by a model running on your own computer via Ollama — nothing is sent to the cloud.

1
Make sure Ollama is installed and running on your computer (look for the llama icon in your system tray).
2
Open Terminal from the top nav bar.
3
Type ask <your question> or alfred <your question> and press Enter.
4
Alfred's reply streams in below your question, right in the Terminal log.
Opening Ollama's own chat window
Alfred (above) talks to Ollama automatically in the background — you never need to open Ollama yourself for normal use. But if you ever want to chat with the model directly, outside of Canopus:

1. Open the Ollama app from your Start menu (Windows) or Applications (Mac) — this is the same app you installed, separate from Canopus.
2. Its window has a chat box built in — type a model name (e.g. llama3.2:1b) at the top if prompted, then chat directly.
3. This chat is completely separate from Alfred in Canopus — closing it does not stop Ollama from running in the background, so Alfred will keep working as long as the tray icon is present.

Alfred says "unreachable"? Open Command Prompt and run:
set OLLAMA_ORIGINS=* then ollama serve
Keep that window open — this is the most reliable fix if the tray app alone doesn't work.

Alfred feels slow to respond? By default Ollama unloads the model after 5 minutes idle, so the next question has to reload it first. To keep it loaded longer, run before ollama serve:
set OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m
